extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent litigators, and law students studying U.S. patent equity practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when equity jurisdiction exists (or is absent) in patent infringement suits and on the nature, elements, pleading, and procedural treatment of the principal equitable and statutory defenses in such suits. Covers laches, jurisdictional rules, and which of the enumerated statutory defenses must be pleaded and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable jurisdiction — when it exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-jurisdiction in equity is a defence which will succeed in any infringement case, unless an injunction is granted, or at least rightfully prayed for in that case, or unless some impediment prevents a resort to remedies purely legal, or unless the circumstances of the case render the remedy obtainable by an action at law difficult, inadequate, or incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: equity appropriate where legal remedies are inadequate or impossible. Courts look to whether a proper case for injunction is stated and properly prayed for; if so, equity should retain jurisdiction even if later events make an injunction impossible. If the bill untruly states such a case, jurisdiction will lapse and be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity absent when patent expired before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity jurisdiction is therefore absent where the patent expired before the bill is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if an expired and unexpired patent are alleged to be combined in one machine so that apportionment of damages/profits is practically impossible, equitable relief may be stated. Also, patents pertaining to same subject-matter between same parties may be in equity if they can be tried on same record even though some nearly expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable title by executory contract insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the complainant has no ownership in the patent at the time when the bill was filed, equitable jurisdiction is also absent. Equitable title to a patent arising out of an executory contract to assign the patent to the plaintiff is not sufficient to confer jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bill must show ownership (or sufficient equitable title that constitutes an impediment to legal remedy) at filing to sustain equity jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of equity when bill filed before expiration and properly pleads injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: But where a bill is filed before the expiration of the patent upon which it is based, and where it truly states a proper case for an injunction, and contains a proper prayer for that relief, equity has jurisdiction, and should retain it to the end of the suit; even if, on account of the expiration of the patent before a hearing, or sale of the patent by the complainant before a hearing is obtained, or on account of public policy, or on account of the complainant's delay, no injunction is ever granted in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing before expiration and properly stating/praying for injunction preserves equity jurisdiction despite later events that prevent issuance of an injunction (subject to court discretion and public policy concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal where bill filed too shortly before expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bill is filed so shortly before the expiration of the patent that no motion for an injunction can be regularly notified to the defendant and heard by the court till after that expiration, the bill will be dismissed whenever the court learns that no injunction can be lawfully granted. And where a bill states no ground for a preliminary injunction, and is filed so shortly before the expiration of the patent that no permanent injunction can possibly be obtained in the case, the bill will also be dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of filing relative to patent expiration is crucial; courts may dismiss where judicial process cannot allow lawful injunction before expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untruthful pleading of injunction grounds causes dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: But where a bill untruly states a proper case for an injunction, and contains a prayer for that relief, the jurisdiction of equity will lapse and the bill be dismissed whenever it is shown to have been untrue in respect of those of its statements upon which the prayer for an injunction is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material misstatements supporting a prayer for equitable relief are fatal to equity jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior adjudication at law not required for equity jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior adjudication in an action at law is not necessary to give jurisdiction to equity in cases of infringements of patents. A district court may, in its discretion, order a trial at law in such a case, or order a trial by jury at its own bar, in order to inform the conscience of the chancellor; but no such trial can be demanded by either party as an absolute right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity courts are technically competent to decide facts; court may call a legal trial to assist but it's discretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches — equitable defense and its elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches is a defence peculiar to courts of equity. They proceed on the assumption that the party to whom laches is imputed has knowledge of his rights and ample opportunity to establish them; that by reason of his delay the adverse party has good reason to believe the rights are worthless or abandoned; and that due to change in condition/relations during delay it would be an injustice to permit assertion now. Length of time varies with circumstances; time alone is not a test. There must be something practically amounting to an equitable estoppel (e.g., investment by defendant in infringing business with plaintiff's knowledge and inaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay may be excused if harmless, if complainant did not know of infringement, if litigating a test case, if infringer was warned and patentee preparing action. Courts examine facts; whether complainant or assignor charged with laches matters. To guard against laches, bills should state excuses for delay and evidence should support them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading/explaining delay to avoid laches defense
rubrics_metrics.description: To guard against a motion to dismiss based on laches where long delay intervened between infringement and filing, the bill ought to state the existing excuses for that delay; and evidence ought to show whatever excuse the complainant can interpose. This is absolutely essential in a bill for infringement of a broadened reissue where it appears that a delay of more than two years intervened between issuance of the original patent and application for the reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmatively plead and prove reasons for delay when significant time elapsed, especially in reissue contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses based on the face of the patent may be moved to dismiss
rubrics_metrics.description: The first of the twenty-seven defences ... can be made in a motion to dismiss, where the letters patent appear on their face to have been granted for something other than a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or design. And indeed any defence which can be based upon the face of the patent can be made by motion to dismiss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invalidity is apparent from patent record itself (e.g., wrong statutory subject matter), defendant may move to dismiss without traversing merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of invention (lack of inventive step) — judicial notice and pleading
rubrics_metrics.description: The second defence may be made on the hearing, without any pleading or evidence, in all cases where the court will take judicial notice of the fact which shows want of invention; and a motion to dismiss will also be sustained in the same circumstances. But a court will not take judicial notice of a fact merely because it is stated in a prior patent nor of any fact which is not generally known, nor of any fact the reality or significance of which is subject to doubt. A motion to dismiss for want of invention will be denied except in a clear case. Where the state of the prior art must be proved by evidence, it is necessary to set up the defence of want of invention in an answer. But the answer need not state the particular part of the prior art upon which the defence is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of invention can support dismissal only when obvious on common knowledge or patent face; otherwise must be pleaded and proved in answer; courts require clear cases for summary dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on judicial notice for prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A court will not take judicial notice of a fact merely because it is stated in a prior patent; nor of any fact which is not generally known, even though known to the judge; nor of any fact the reality or the significance of which is subject to doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior-art facts generally require evidentiary proof unless they are indisputable and generally known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to dismiss not sustained by patent's recital of prior art absent estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to dismiss will not be sustained, in such a case, on the basis of what the patent may set forth as the state of the prior art; unless the patentee is some way estopped from showing the patent to be otherwise than accurate in its statements on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent's own recitation about prior art cannot be used to preclude patentee from rebutting absent estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may sua sponte declare patent invalid where absence of invention clearly appears on face
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been held that where absence of invention clearly appears on the face of the patent itself, the court may, even though the question is not raised by the pleadings, sua sponte, declare the patent invalid and dismiss the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme cases may allow court to act on its own motion when invalidity is indisputable from patent text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of novelty — must be pleaded and statutory notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The third defence could never be set up in a plea, because the statute expressly provides that it shall be set up in an answer. Nor can it be based on such a notice as will effect the purpose in an action at law. It has always required an answer for its embodiment; and that answer must state the same things which a statutory notice of want of novelty in an action at law is required to contain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of want of novelty taken without proper pleading may be inadmissible or admissible in the court's discretion; historically, subsequent proper notice and time (e.g., 30 days before trial) could cure defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of evidence on want of novelty when answer asserts it
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the answer states that the patent sued on is void for want of novelty, evidence to support that statement will be admitted at the hearing, though not specified in the answer, unless the complainant objects to that evidence for want of the statutory notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A properly framed answer asserting lack of novelty enables admission of supporting evidence unless procedural statutory notice defects are raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (lack of utility) not proper for plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth defence is not rightly the subject-matter of a plea, for though a defendant may make an oath that he believes the patented thing to be without utility, he can hardly swear that it is certainly so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to utility require more than a defendant's oath; must be raised in appropriate pleading (answer) and proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences based on abandonment require answer with factual particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifth and sixth defences, even before the present Equity Rules were proper only for an answer, because they both rest on evidence of abandonment outside of the bill, and therefore cannot be interposed by a demurrer or motion to dismiss. Being two of the five defences provided for by Section 4920 of the Revised Statutes, neither of them are proper subject-matter of a plea. And an answer must show what fact or facts constitute the abandonment which is invoked therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment defenses demand affirmative factual pleading in the answer describing the abandonment acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh defence (claim not in original application) requires claim construction and proof — answer only
rubrics_metrics.description: The seventh defence involves whether the letters patent claim something not indicated or described in the specification or drawings of the original application; the question what letters patent claim is a question of law for the court and to decide it the original application must be introduced as evidence. Therefore the defence cannot be raised by plea, demurrer, or motion to dismiss and is properly set up only in the answer (except where complainant takes the initiative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because resolution requires claim construction and comparison with the original application, it must be litigated with evidence in an answer; complainant may bear burden where he raised the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighth defence must be set up in answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The eighth defence is one of the five which the statute requires to be set up in an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory list of defenses (e.g., Section 4920) prescribes that certain defenses be asserted by answer rather than plea/motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth and tenth defences (joint or sole invention) — may be pleaded if defendant has knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the ninth or the tenth defence may be treated as pleas where the defendant knows the fact of joint or of sole invention upon which they respectively stand. Each rests upon a single matter of fact which, if decided against the complainant, is fatal to his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant has personal knowledge of inventorship facts, these defenses can be pleaded; otherwise typical practice is to assert in answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleventh defence — detailed facts required in answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The eleventh defence stands in the same category, in respect of equity pleading, with the third, fifth, sixth, and eighth, and the answer must state the details of the facts upon which the eleventh defence is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed factual allegations in the answer for this defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelfth defence (insufficiency of specification) cannot be pleaded by motion or plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The twelfth defence cannot be made by a motion to dismiss; and it cannot be treated as a plea because, though the defendant might be able to make oath that he is a person skilled in the art and that the description contained in that patent is not full, clear, concise, and exact enough to enable him to make and use the same, he could not make oath that the same thing is true of other persons skilled in that art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement/insufficiency challenges require proof beyond defendant's oath and must be raised by answer and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thirteenth defence (claim construction) — not a plea but may be moved to dismiss if patent is proferted
rubrics_metrics.description: The thirteenth defence cannot be treated as a plea because it depends on the construction of the claims of the letters patent, and not upon any matter of fact to be sworn to in a plea or proved in a deposition. But this defence can be made by a motion to dismiss where profert has been made of the letters patent, or they have otherwise been made a part of the bill. An answer was formerly a proper pleading in which to interpose this defence, and of course it is so now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the patent is part of the bill (profert), claim-construction-based defenses may justify a motion to dismiss; otherwise raise in answer with evidence.
